title: The Timeline
eyebrow: Lives against the state that governed them
dek: Who this family were living under, and what it did to them. The point is not when people were born — it is what was happening around them when they were.

bands.label: Before the surname
bands.note: The hamlet of Swanhunger is in the free-warren charters of Henry II, Richard I, John and Edward I, and a family takes its name from it. This band is here because the archive's evidence now reaches it, not because the family line does — nothing joins these people to the Sanigers of the registers.

bands.label: Tudor and Stuart Gloucestershire
bands.note: The muster of 1608, the Berkeley estate deeds, and Smyth of Nibley writing the survey of the hundred in about 1639. The surname is in all three, in eight spellings, two centuries before the parish registers this archive reads.

bands.label: Georgian Britain
bands.note: Robert D'Arcy's whole life, and his son's first thirty-five years. A standing army, a global war every twenty years, and a Board of Ordnance that commissioned engineers without recording where they came from.

bands.label: Convict New South Wales
bands.note: Transportation. It is what brought this family to Australia: not free settlement but a garrison posting aboard a convict ship.

bands.label: Colonial Queensland
bands.note: Separation from New South Wales. A new colony needed a Government Printing Office, a gaol, an electric telegraph and a police force, and this family staffed all four.

bands.label: The Commonwealth
bands.note: Federation, then two wars that took four men out of one family.

events.what: A lord Berkeley grants the monastery “one yard land at Swonhunger”
Thomas de Swonhungre is named as the son of Thomas de Esshelesworth — a locative surname at the moment it becomes heritable
Thomas de Swonhunger contracts with the chaplain of Kingley, on Easter day
Thomas de Stone dies leaving two daughters. Wanswell is allotted to ALICE, who marries John Swanhunger; her elder sister Joan takes Stone and Woodford
A charter executed AT SANIGER describes the path to SWONHUNGRE and is witnessed by a man surnamed de Swonhungre — the two names in one sentence, three centuries before Smyth
John de Swonhongre rides in Maurice de Berkeley's retinue, as an esquire
Alice and Joan settle their father's inheritance; the deed names ELYANORA DE STONE, «mother of the aforesaid Alice and Joan»
Three coheirs divide the inheritance of John de Wyke in Ham — Joan Capel, ALICE DE SWONHONGRE and Agnes de Lorewynge, each named as the ancestor her heir holds through
William, brother and heir of Thomas de Swonhunger, partitions the family lands in Ham, Cam, Stinchcombe, Kingscote and Haselcote — «except the fishery in Severn, which will remain in common»
John Sergeant endows a chantry at Stone to pray for «William son of William Swanhangre, and ALIENOR his mother»
Thomas lord Berkeley sells the marriage of John Swonhongre, «which came to Thomas because Elias held of Thomas BY KNIGHT SERVICE» — the tenure, in the lord's own words
John Swonhonger is aged 18, by a royal inquisition taken on the Daubeney inheritance
John Swonhungre dies without issue; the main line ends in two sisters
A John Swonhungre holds two shops with gardens in the Market at Bristol
Robert Saniger buys a manor from William Lord Stourton
The court baron of the manor of Ham and Hinton sits — in John Smyth of Nibley's own collection, now at Birmingham, and not yet read
John Saniger of Berkeley, yeoman — the earliest dated document naming the surname
Eleven men of the surname mustered in Gloucestershire; John Sainger, weaver, lives in the hamlet itself
Smyth of Nibley: “Swonhunger; corruptly called Saniger”
Edward Saniger of Saniger, clothier; a gentleman by 1709
Saniger Farm «was sold by EDWARD SANIGER to the Earl of Berkeley» — J. H. Cooke's claim, and the join this archive cannot yet document
Robert D'Arcy commissioned Practitioner Engineer and 2nd Lieutenant, 17 January
Marries Jean Ward at Portsea, 21 June
Lieutenant Robert D'Arcy at the siege of Fort St Philip's, Minorca
A son christened at St Michael, Barbados — the Corps posted men across the empire
Constantine D'Arcy dies at Chatham
Lieutenant-Colonel R. D'Arcy, Commanding Engineer of the Copenhagen expedition
Walcheren: arrested at Flushing for refusing to write a report
George Pitt D'Arcy at Orthes, with the 39th Foot
The convict ship England sails: a Major of the 39th, 39 men, 6 women, 7 children, and Mrs D'Arcy in the cabin
Robert D'Arcy dies at Chatham, 13 May. His will is proved 4 July and has never been read
Samuel Charles Sneyd arrives with the 4th (King's Own)
Marries Catherine Margaret Mulcahy at Camden, 13 February
The Chubb capture — a sergeant of the Mounted Police
Major George Pitt D'Arcy dies at Parramatta — “gout which had flown to the head”
Lydia Sanigar dies at Berkeley — register 3, entry 265
Queensland separates from New South Wales. Samuel Sneyd becomes Governor of Brisbane Gaol
William Hartley Sneyd enters the public service, 1 February — the Government Printing Office
Paul Cole Atkinson installs the first organ at All Saints', Wickham Terrace, and plays it
William Hartley Sneyd is insolvent
He is found dead in Victoria Park. His widow's deposition names his father and closes a generation
Three Sneyds and a D'Arcy enlist
Arthur Hartley Sneyd killed at Pozières. Six men give six accounts
Vivian Claude Sneyd wins a Bar to the Military Medal at Westhoek
Lindesay Atkinson D'Arcy dies suddenly at 44, of Botany Street, Clayfield
Kenneth Lindsay D'Arcy's eulogy, delivered in three parts by his three children

close: The bands are the state, not the family. Read the two together and the pattern is hard to miss: this family goes where a government sends it, and gets written down when a government writes it down.
